stories.headline: Tulsi Gabbard Resigns as Director of National Intelligence After Husband's Cancer Diagnosis
stories.summary:
Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard announced her resignation Friday, effective June 30, citing her husband Abraham Williams's recent diagnosis with an extremely rare form of bone cancer. Gabbard informed President Trump of her decision in a White House meeting and submitted a formal resignation letter, saying she could not "in good conscience" ask her husband to face the illness alone while she remained in a demanding government role. ODNI Principal Deputy Director Aaron Lukas will serve as acting director.

President Trump praised Gabbard on Truth Social, saying she "has done an incredible job" and expressing confidence that her husband would recover. The ODNI confirmed her departure was for "personal reasons." Gabbard has served as the nation's top intelligence official since her Senate confirmation in February 2025.

During her tenure, Gabbard oversaw the declassification of more than half a million pages of government records, including documents related to the Trump-Russia investigation and the assassination of President John F. Kennedy. In her resignation letter she cited "significant progress" at the ODNI in "advancing unprecedented transparency and restoring integrity to the intelligence community."

Reuters reported, citing a source familiar with the matter, that Gabbard was forced out by the White House rather than departing voluntarily — a claim a senior administration official denied, calling it "total bulls***" to the Washington Examiner. Gabbard is the latest in a series of Trump Cabinet departures, following former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and former Attorney General Pam Bondi, both of whom were ousted by Trump.

stories.headline: Update: New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Sworn In Amid Inflation Pressures and Trump Rate-Cut Demands
stories.summary:
Kevin Warsh was sworn in Friday at the White House as the 17th Chairman of the Federal Reserve, beginning his tenure against a backdrop of elevated inflation, an energy price shock stemming from the ongoing Strait of Hormuz crisis, and intense political pressure from President Trump to lower interest rates. Former Fed Governor Betsy Duke described both Warsh and outgoing Chair Jerome Powell as "natural leaders" while acknowledging the challenging conditions Warsh inherits.

Warsh faces a Federal Reserve board that is broadly skeptical of near-term rate cuts, complicating any effort to accommodate the president's wishes. Fed minutes released previously showed a majority of officials open to rate hikes if inflation persists — directly at odds with Trump's public demands for lower borrowing costs. Trump himself urged Warsh on Friday to make independent decisions: "Don't look at me, don't look at anybody."

The transition marks a pivotal moment for U.S. monetary policy. Warsh, a former Fed governor who served during the 2008 financial crisis, is seen as more hawkish than some Trump allies had hoped. Markets and economists will be watching closely for signals on whether he will resist White House pressure or begin laying groundwork for eventual cuts.

stories.headline: Mahmoud Khalil to Ask Supreme Court to Halt Deportation After Appeals Court Ruling
stories.summary:
Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia University graduate student detained by U.S. authorities over his involvement in pro-Palestinian campus protests, will ask the U.S. Supreme Court to halt his deportation after a federal appeals court on Friday rejected his request for a rehearing. The appeals court's ruling means Khalil must pursue his constitutional claims through the immigration appeals process once a final removal order is issued.

Khalil became a prominent symbol of the Trump administration's crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrators. His case has drawn intense scrutiny from civil liberties advocates, who argue that his detention raises First Amendment concerns, and from immigration enforcement advocates, who contend the government has broad discretion to deport non-citizens on national security grounds.

The move to the Supreme Court represents a significant escalation of a case that has drawn national attention to the limits of free speech protections for non-citizen protesters. The high court has not yet indicated whether it will take up the matter, and Khalil's legal team faces a narrow procedural window to seek an emergency stay of removal.

stories.headline: Explosion and Fire at Staten Island Shipyard Injures 16, Including Firefighters
stories.summary:
A fire and explosion at a Staten Island, New York, shipyard injured at least 16 people Friday afternoon, including three with serious injuries, according to the New York Fire Department. The incident began around 3:30 p.m. when workers were reported trapped in a confined space at a dock; firefighters arrived to find a blaze burning in the basement of a large metal structure. A major explosion occurred approximately 50 minutes into the response, injuring two firefighters and one civilian seriously, with two additional firefighters sustaining moderate injuries.

More than 200 firefighters and emergency medical personnel from 68 units responded to the scene. The cause of the fire and explosion remains under investigation. The dock is home to several businesses, including a coffee roasting company and a self-storage facility, and the shipyard is the former site of Bethlehem Steel Company operations used to build U.S. Navy vessels during World War II.

stories.headline: Federal Judge Dismisses Human Smuggling Case Against Kilmar Abrego Garcia, Citing Vindictive Prosecution
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Tennessee dismissed all criminal charges against Kilmar Abrego Garcia on Friday, ruling that the Trump administration had prosecuted him for political reasons rather than on the merits of the evidence. U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw wrote that the case was brought only to justify the government's earlier wrongful deportation of Abrego Garcia to El Salvador, and that prosecutors had failed to rebut a legal presumption of vindictiveness. "The objective evidence here shows that, absent Abrego's successful lawsuit challenging his removal to El Salvador, the government would not have brought this prosecution," Crenshaw wrote.

Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who had lived in Maryland for years and is married to an American citizen, was wrongfully deported to El Salvador's CECOT megaprison in March 2025 despite a standing court order protecting him from removal. The Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate his return. He was brought back to the U.S. in June 2025 only after federal prosecutors filed human smuggling charges against him related to a 2022 Tennessee traffic stop in which several people were found in his vehicle. He had pleaded not guilty.

The Justice Department had maintained the prosecution was apolitical and that charges were brought because "the evidence pointed to Abrego Garcia having committed a crime." The department had not commented on Friday's dismissal as of publication. Supporters of the administration argued the charges were legitimate and that Abrego Garcia had evaded accountability; immigration enforcement critics argued the case exemplified the use of criminal charges as a tool of political retaliation.

The ruling is the latest development in a high-profile legal saga that has become a central flashpoint in debates over the limits of executive power in immigration enforcement. The case is covered by nine outlets and marks a concrete new legal outcome in an ongoing story.

stories.headline: DHS Orders Green Card Applicants to Return to Home Countries Before Seeking Permanent U.S. Residency
stories.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security announced Friday that immigrants currently in the United States on temporary visas — including students, tourist visa holders, and temporary workers — must return to their home countries before applying for permanent legal residency (green cards), with exceptions only in "extraordinary circumstances." The policy reverses a longstanding practice that allowed applicants to adjust their status from within the U.S. DHS characterized the existing process as a "loophole" that incentivizes abuse of the immigration system.

"An alien who is in the U.S. temporarily and wants a Green Card must return to their home country to apply," DHS said in a statement. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesman Zach Kahler said the change frees USCIS resources to process other visa categories, including visas for victims of violent crime and human trafficking, and ensures the system functions "as the law intended." The administration framed the move as part of its broader effort to reduce overall immigration levels.

Critics of the policy argue it will force hundreds of thousands of legal visa holders — many of whom have lived and worked in the U.S. for years — to uproot themselves and potentially face lengthy waits abroad before receiving a determination. Immigration attorneys warn that consular processing timelines are already severely backlogged, meaning applicants could face years outside the country. The change affects a wide population including foreign workers at major corporations, international students who marry U.S. citizens, and others with lawful temporary status.

The announcement comes as the administration reported that ICE and federal partners have arrested 641,000 undocumented immigrants since January 2025, with 800,000 removed. The green card guidance is covered by six outlets and represents a significant new federal policy action with broad impact on the legal immigration system.

stories.headline: Thousands Ordered to Evacuate in Orange County, California Over Unstable Toxic Chemical Tank
stories.summary:
Southern California officials expanded evacuation orders Friday across several Orange County cities after a tank containing a toxic substance became "actively in crisis," with authorities warning of a possible explosion or spill. The precise chemical involved and the location of the facility were not fully detailed in early reports, but officials described the situation as rapidly deteriorating and urged residents in affected zones to leave immediately.

Emergency response teams were deployed to the site as officials worked to stabilize the tank. The evacuation zone expansion suggests the threat radius grew during the day, affecting an unknown but potentially large number of residents in the densely populated Southern California county. Orange County has a population of more than 3 million people.

The incident is in early stages of reporting, covered by two outlets as of Friday afternoon. Authorities have not confirmed casualties or indicated whether the tank failure was accidental or the result of equipment malfunction. Further updates are expected as emergency crews assess the situation on the ground.

stories.headline: IRS Grants Trump Sweeping Tax Audit Immunity in Unusual Settlement, Experts Warn of Unprecedented Scope
stories.summary:
The Internal Revenue Service has agreed to permanently drop all pending tax probes of President Donald Trump, his sons, and the Trump Organization as part of a settlement resolving Trump's $10 billion lawsuit over the 2018 leak of his tax returns to The New York Times. A one-page court document states the U.S. government is "forever barred and precluded" from examining or prosecuting Trump's or the Trump Organization's current tax filings — a provision quietly added to a broader $1.8 billion settlement establishing a fund to compensate people Trump alleges were improperly investigated.

Tax and legal experts are calling the grant of immunity extraordinary in its breadth. Former IRS Commissioner Daniel Werfel said the settlement was "an unprecedented remedy," adding that Trump should be subject to the same enforcement framework as any other American. Among the probes potentially shelved is a long-standing audit into whether Trump double-dipped on tax deductions — a technique that could have triggered an estimated $100 million liability if wrongdoing had been found.

Trump has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and characterized IRS scrutiny as politically motivated, without providing evidence. Supporters argue the original leak of his tax returns was itself an illegal government act that warranted legal remedy. Critics, including Democratic lawmakers and tax law scholars, contend that having a president sue — and then effectively immunize himself from — an agency within his own administration sets a dangerous precedent for equal enforcement of tax law.

The arrangement is structurally unusual: Trump sued a federal agency overseen by his own executive branch, and that agency then resolved the case in his favor with what experts describe as a uniquely broad shield against future examination.

stories.headline: Putin Vows Retaliation After Accusing Ukraine of Striking Student Dormitory in Occupied Luhansk
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered his military to prepare retaliatory options after accusing Ukraine of a drone strike on a student dormitory in Starobilsk, in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine. Putin said six people were killed and 39 injured in the overnight attack, which he described as carried out in three waves using 16 drones, and that 15 people remained missing. Kremlin-installed officials released images showing a collapsed building with rescuers searching the rubble.

Ukraine's military acknowledged the strike but offered a different characterization, saying it had targeted the headquarters of Russia's elite Rubicon drone unit, which it accused of regularly attacking Ukrainian civilians and civilian infrastructure. Ukraine stated its forces strictly adhere to international humanitarian law and that the building served military purposes. The BBC was unable to independently verify the nature of the structure or the casualty figures.

The strike escalates an already intense period of cross-border attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukrainian forces had also struck an FSB headquarters in the Russian-occupied Kherson region, killing or wounding approximately 100 Russian personnel. Russia's military has not confirmed that incident. Last week, a Russian missile strike destroyed a residential high-rise in Kyiv, killing 24 people including three children.

Putin's vow of retaliation raises concerns about a further escalation in the conflict. Russia has consistently denied deliberately targeting civilians, while Ukraine accuses Moscow of a systematic campaign against civilian infrastructure since its full-scale invasion began in February 2022.

stories.headline: Update: Cuba's Blackouts and Fuel Shortages Deepen as U.S. Pressure Intensifies
stories.summary:
Cubans are enduring up to 20-hour daily blackouts and severe fuel shortages as the United States maintains a near-total fuel blockade on the island. Residents in Havana high-rises describe being unable to leave their apartments due to non-functioning elevators, with elderly and medically vulnerable residents including those with pacemakers facing heightened danger. Water delivery to over 100 residents in one building has effectively ceased.

The crisis coincides with escalating U.S. pressure following the formal indictment of former Cuban leader Raúl Castro over the 1996 shootdown of Brothers to the Rescue aircraft that killed four people, including three Americans. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has declared Cuba a "national security threat" and characterized the chances of a peaceful resolution as "not high." Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel dismissed the charges as "a political manoeuvre, devoid of any legal foundation."

President Trump has publicly discussed toppling Cuba's communist government. U.S. demands reportedly include political and economic reforms and an end to Russian and Chinese intelligence presence on the island, though the specifics remain unclear. The combination of sanctions, indictments, and fuel restrictions represents the most intensive U.S. campaign against Cuba in decades.

Many Cubans were unaware of the Castro indictment when it was announced due to the ongoing communications blackouts. The humanitarian conditions described on the ground illustrate the direct civilian toll of the geopolitical standoff, a dimension that critics of the policy have emphasized.

stories.headline: Waymo Pauses Robotaxi Service in Five U.S. Cities After Vehicles Drive Into Flooded Roads
stories.summary:
Alphabet-owned Waymo has suspended its self-driving taxi service across five U.S. cities — four in Texas and Atlanta — after multiple incidents in which vehicles entered flooded roads and became stranded. The company also separately paused freeway operations in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Miami while evaluating vehicle performance in construction zones. Waymo provides more than 500,000 trips per week across its U.S. markets.

The pause follows a voluntary recall of nearly 3,800 robotaxis using the company's fifth and sixth-generation automated driving systems, disclosed to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration earlier this month. A key incident occurred April 20 in San Antonio, where an unoccupied Waymo vehicle entered a flooded road and was swept into a creek. A similar incident was recorded in Atlanta on Wednesday.

Waymo said it is working on "additional software safeguards" to prevent vehicles from slowing and then driving into standing water on higher-speed roadways. The company said safety was its "highest priority" and that it expected to resume affected routes soon. Waymo had been planning to launch a London service later this year.

The incidents add to a series of high-profile autonomous vehicle failures over the past year, including a major San Francisco power outage in December 2025 that halted Waymo service citywide and a mass Apollo Go robotaxi outage in Wuhan, China in April that stopped over 100 vehicles mid-traffic. Regulators and safety advocates have used such incidents to press for clearer federal oversight standards for autonomous vehicles.

stories.headline: U.S. Sanctions Senior Tanzanian Police Official Over Torture and Sexual Assault of Rights Activists
stories.summary:
The United States has sanctioned Faustine Jackson Mafwele, Tanzania's senior assistant commissioner of police, over his alleged involvement in the detention, torture, and sexual assault of Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan activist Agather Atuhaire in May 2025. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the designation, which bars Mafwele from entering the United States, citing "credible information" of gross human rights violations. He is the first senior official under President Samia Suluhu Hassan's government to face foreign sanctions.

The two activists had traveled to Tanzania to observe the trial of opposition leader Tundu Lissu when they were detained. Mwangi alleged he was stripped, hung upside down, beaten on his feet, and sexually assaulted; Atuhaire said she was raped. Tanzanian police previously dismissed the allegations as "opinions" and "hearsay." A BBC Africa Eye documentary in February named Mafwele as the main perpetrator; he did not respond to those allegations.

The sanctions come amid broader scrutiny of Tanzania following a disputed October general election in which a commission of inquiry found 518 people died — 197 shot dead — during ensuing protests. The commission blamed foreign-sponsored groups for the violence, a characterization rejected by opposition figures and human rights organizations who attribute the deaths to security forces.

Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have both cited the activists' case in pressing for accountability. U.S. lawmakers had called for tougher action on Tanzania's human rights record. Tanzania's Foreign Affairs Ministry said it had not yet received the formal designation.

stories.headline: Update: Iran's Strait of Hormuz Blockade Sends Gas Prices to $4.53 as Global Shipping Collapses
stories.summary:
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen by as much as 97% since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran on February 28, according to vessel-tracking data. Iranian threats to fire drones and ballistic missiles at ships that do not comply with its demands have effectively halted the waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's daily oil supply previously moved. The national average gasoline price has risen to $4.53 per gallon, up from $2.98 two days before the conflict began, according to AAA.

The Strait is roughly 20 nautical miles wide at its narrowest point between Oman and Iran, making vessels particularly vulnerable to Iranian forces operating within or near the country's 12-nautical-mile territorial sea. International maritime law — including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea — requires freedom of passage through such straits, but enforcement has proven difficult under active conflict conditions. From a peak of up to 180 vessels transiting daily before the strikes, traffic collapsed within hours of the initial attacks.

The disruption has raised urgent questions about the global economy's vulnerability to chokepoint strategy and what leverage any negotiated ceasefire would actually provide, given that Iran retains the capability to reimpose the blockade. U.S. officials have said they are in the final stages of an Iran deal, though no agreement has been announced. The blockade's economic ripple effects extend well beyond oil, touching liquefied natural gas shipments and broader trade flows across Asia, Europe, and the Americas.

The story is covered by 15 outlets spanning the ideological spectrum, making it among the most broadly reported international developments of the day. Critics of the administration argue the military strikes precipitated an avoidable economic crisis, while supporters contend the pressure campaign is necessary to dismantle Iran's nuclear and military ambitions.

stories.headline: Turkey's Top Court Voids Opposition Party Leadership Election, Sparking 'Judicial Coup' Accusations
stories.summary:
Turkey's appeals court on Thursday declared the 2023 internal leadership election of the Republican People's Party (CHP) — the country's main opposition bloc — null and void, effectively removing party leader Özgür Özel and the entire party executive. The ruling installs in their place Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, the 77-year-old veteran whom Özel defeated and who was himself beaten by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in the 2023 presidential election. Thousands of demonstrators gathered outside CHP headquarters in Ankara following the decision.

Özel denounced the ruling as a 'judicial coup' and said the party's executive had rejected the court's authority. 'These coup plotters don't come with tanks, cannons, rifles or camouflage; these coup plotters come in judges' and prosecutors' robes,' he said. Turkey's Justice Minister Akin Gürlek — who was appointed by Erdoğan earlier this year and previously served as the chief prosecutor leading corruption investigations against the opposition and jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoğlu — defended the ruling as reinforcing public trust in democracy.

Turkey's stock market fell 6% late Thursday before partially recovering Friday morning. The CHP's supreme election council appeal was being heard Friday, though legal challenges through Turkey's Court of Cassation are expected to be prolonged. The ruling further concentrates power around Erdoğan, who has governed Turkey since 2003 and faces constitutional constraints on running for president again without early elections or constitutional changes.

The decision follows a pattern of legal pressure on the opposition that has included Imamoğlu's imprisonment on corruption charges. Western governments and democracy monitors have previously raised concerns about judicial independence in Turkey under Erdoğan's administration, while Turkish government officials maintain the court system operates independently and within the rule of law.

stories.headline: Trump Announces 5,000 Additional Troops for Poland as NATO Foreign Ministers Meet in Sweden
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Thursday that the United States will send an additional 5,000 troops to Poland, one week after the Pentagon abruptly cancelled a planned deployment of 4,000 troops to the country. Trump attributed the decision to his personal relationship with Polish President Karol Nawrocki, whom he backed in last year's elections. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte welcomed the announcement ahead of a foreign ministers' summit in Helsingborg, Sweden.

The reversal comes amid considerable uncertainty about U.S. troop posture in Europe. Earlier this month, Washington announced the withdrawal of 5,000 troops from Germany following a dispute between Trump and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz over the war with Iran. It remains unclear whether the Poland deployment draws from those Germany-based forces or represents a separate commitment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had characterized last week's Poland cancellation as only 'a temporary delay.'

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters en route to the NATO summit, said Trump remains 'very upset and disappointed' with some alliance members over their response to U.S. operations in the Middle East. Rubio indicated burden-sharing would be a central topic at the Helsingborg talks and declined to rule out further reductions in U.S. troop availability for NATO's collective defense commitments. The White House has broadly signaled an intent to reduce its European military footprint as part of its America First agenda.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul welcomed the Poland deployment as serving 'the security of the whole alliance,' even as Berlin navigates a strained relationship with Washington. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the announcement 'good news for both countries.' The episode illustrates the volatile and relationship-driven nature of current U.S. alliance management, which allies and critics say creates planning uncertainty for NATO's eastern flank.

stories.headline: Pentagon Releases Second Batch of Declassified UFO Files, Including 1969 Apollo 12 Astronaut Audio
stories.summary:
The Pentagon published 222 declassified files Friday related to unidentified anomalous phenomena, the second such release following a presidential order by Trump directing the declassification of government UFO records. Among the documents is audio from a 1969 post-mission medical debrief in which Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad, Richard Gordon, and Alan Bean described experiencing mysterious 'streaks of light' while attempting to sleep in deep space, despite having their eyes closed. NASA's medical team at the time concluded the phenomenon was caused by the astronauts' own vision rather than external light sources.

The release also includes 116 pages of documentation tied to alleged sightings at a top-secret facility in Sandia, New Mexico, between 1948 and 1950, covering 209 reported sightings of 'green orbs,' discs, and fireballs near the military installation. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in a statement that such documents have 'long fueled speculation' and that 'it's time the American people see it for themselves.' The first batch, released May 8, included footage of an 'eight-pointed star' object and Apollo 17 crew reports of unidentified bright sparks in space.

The Department of War said a third batch of files is currently being prepared for release. The declassification effort follows years of incremental Pentagon disclosures about UAP sightings reported by military personnel, and congressional pressure for greater transparency on the subject. The documents are published on the Defense Department's dedicated UAP website.

stories.headline: Update: Alberta Announces October Referendum on Whether to Remain in Canada
stories.summary:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced Thursday that the oil-rich province will hold a referendum on October 19 asking voters whether Alberta should remain in Canada or begin the constitutional process toward a binding separation vote. The announcement follows a citizen-led petition that gathered more than 300,000 signatures calling for separation, and a counter-petition with over 400,000 signatures urging Alberta to stay. Smith said she personally will vote to remain and that her government and caucus share that position, but she framed the referendum as a necessary outlet for democratic expression.

The move marks the most significant test of Canadian national unity in decades, echoing Quebec's two independence referendums, the last of which in 1995 ended with a razor-thin 50.58% to 49.22% vote to remain. Alberta's separatist movement has been fueled by longstanding grievances that the province, a major oil producer, is ignored by federal decision-makers in Ottawa. Opinion polls currently suggest a majority of Albertans would vote against separation.

Smith's announcement was partly triggered by a court ruling that threw out the original separation petition after indigenous First Nations groups argued they had not been properly consulted. Smith said she would not allow 'a legal mistake by a single judge' to silence hundreds of thousands of Albertans. Prime Minister Mark Carney has previously stated that any separation attempt must follow the Clarity Act, the federal law governing the rules for provincial secession.

Separatist advocates reacted with skepticism to Smith's framing of the referendum question, with lawyer Jeffrey Rath writing on social media that Smith 'dealt a referendum question from the bottom of the deck' and had 'just lost her base.' The outcome of October's vote will determine whether a formal, binding referendum on independence moves forward — a process that would trigger complex constitutional and legal negotiations involving the federal government and indigenous nations.

stories.headline: Update: DNC Chair Ken Martin Faces Resignation Calls After Botched Release of 2024 Election Autopsy
stories.summary:
Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin is facing intensifying pressure from congressional Democrats, including open calls to resign, following the chaotic release Thursday of the party's long-suppressed 192-page autopsy of its 2024 presidential election defeat. Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.) told Axios that Martin 'should resign,' citing 'his lack of leadership.' Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas) said Martin should 'move on,' adding 'there doesn't seem to be a plan to turn things around and the clock is ticking.'

Martin had originally promised to release the report after winning the DNC chairmanship in early 2025 but reversed course by December, claiming the party needed to focus on 2026 midterm unity rather than relitigating 2024. After months of mounting criticism, he released the document Thursday alongside an apology. The report identifies key demographic losses — including Latino voters, men, and rural communities — but notably omits any discussion of President Biden's age and his late decision not to seek reelection, the rushed elevation of Vice President Harris as the nominee, or the party's internal divisions over the war in Gaza.

The botched rollout compounds existing concerns about the DNC's fundraising performance, which has lagged significantly behind its Republican counterpart. Critics say the incomplete nature of the report — and Martin's initial effort to suppress it — undermines the party's ability to conduct an honest reckoning with its 2024 losses ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Martin has said he is working to weather the storm and indicated he does not intend to step down. Supporters argue the party needs stability rather than another leadership transition, but the public fracture among House Democrats signals that his position remains precarious heading into the midterm election cycle.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Cuba Tensions Escalate as Trump Pushes Arch Approval, Rubio Warns of Military Option
stories.summary:
President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio escalated rhetoric toward Cuba on Thursday, with Rubio telling reporters en route to a NATO summit that the likelihood of a peaceful agreement with Havana is 'not high' and that the U.S. will 'keep doing what we need to do.' Trump, speaking at the White House, said he believes escalation will not be necessary but has repeatedly refused to rule out military action. The developments follow Wednesday's unsealing of a federal indictment charging former Cuban President Raúl Castro with murder over the 1996 shootdown of two civilian aircraft that killed four U.S. nationals.

In a separate but related development Thursday, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of a U.S.-owned port business whose property was confiscated by Fidel Castro's government in 1960, a decision that opens the door for similar claims from other American companies and individuals against Cuba. Cuba's foreign minister accused Rubio of 'lying once again to provoke military aggression,' and President Miguel Díaz-Canel called the Castro charges 'a political manoeuvre, devoid of any legal foundation.'

On the ground in Cuba, the U.S. pressure campaign has contributed to severe humanitarian conditions. Near-total fuel blockades have produced 20-hour daily blackouts affecting millions of Cubans, leaving elderly residents stranded in high-rises, disrupting water supply, and creating dangerous conditions for people with pacemakers and other medical needs. Many Cubans were unaware of the Castro indictment when it was announced due to the communications blackouts.

Analysts and U.S. lawmakers are openly debating whether the Trump administration is building toward a military operation similar to the January capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Florida Sen. Rick Scott said 'the same thing that happened to Maduro should happen to Raúl Castro.' Experts note that while a military extraction is logistically feasible, Castro's role in the current Cuban government is largely symbolic at age 94, and such an operation would carry significant strategic and diplomatic risks.

stories.headline: Update: Prince Andrew Documents Show Queen Elizabeth Pushed His Trade Envoy Appointment With No Formal Vetting
stories.summary:
Newly released British government documents show that the late Queen Elizabeth II was 'very keen' for then-Prince Andrew to be appointed as Britain's special trade envoy in 2001, and that no formal due diligence or vetting process was undertaken before the appointment was made. The documents were released Thursday under legislation passed by Parliament after lawmakers demanded transparency following Andrew's arrest and questioning over allegations that he shared government intelligence reports with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein while serving as trade envoy.

Trade Minister Chris Bryant said in a written statement to Parliament that 'we have found no evidence that a formal due diligence or vetting process was undertaken' and 'no evidence that this was considered.' Constitutional law expert Craig Prescott of Royal Holloway University said the documents confirm that when the queen made her wishes clear, her civil service had little choice but to comply — effectively ending any scrutiny of the appointment.

Andrew, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor after being stripped of his royal titles last year, served as trade envoy from 2001 to 2011 before being forced out over concerns about his ties to questionable figures in Libya and Azerbaijan. The government confirmed it is cooperating with Thames Valley Police on their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor for possible misconduct in public office related to his access to sensitive government reports.

The revelations add to longstanding criticism that Queen Elizabeth's protective instincts toward her second son delayed accountability and damaged the monarchy's reputation. Royal commentators have argued for years that the queen should have moved more quickly to remove Andrew from official duties as allegations about his Epstein ties mounted.
